title: Recommender systems and cold start
summary: From a sparse rating matrix to production recommenders: item-item CF, matrix factorization with SGD and ALS, implicit feedback, two-tower retrieval, cold start and honest evaluation.
outcomes: Compute item-item cosine similarities and a weighted-sum rating prediction by hand
Explain how SGD and ALS fit matrix factorization, and why ALS suits implicit feedback
Explain two-stage retrieval and why in-batch negatives need the logQ correction
Choose cold-start strategies for new items (content, projection) and new users (popularity, bandits)
Spot evaluation pitfalls: random splits, weak baselines and popularity bias

lessons.title: From a sparse rating matrix to item-to-item recommendations

blocks.md:
A recommender answers one question many times a second: of the items this user has not seen, which should we show first? The raw material is a **user-item matrix**: one row per user, one column per item, and a cell filled only where the user interacted. Netflix-style star ratings are *explicit* feedback; clicks, purchases and watch time are *implicit* feedback, which tells you what someone did, not whether they liked it.

The matrix is overwhelmingly empty, because any one user touches a tiny fraction of the catalog. Recommending is filling in the blanks and ranking them.

Two naive answers fail. **Popularity** (show the global top sellers) is a strong baseline but gives every user the same list. **Content filtering** builds a profile from item attributes (genre, author), which needs that metadata and misses tastes it does not describe.

**Collaborative filtering** (CF) uses only behaviour: people who agreed in the past tend to agree again. Koren, Bell and Volinsky note that CF is usually more accurate than content-based methods but suffers from the **cold start problem**: it cannot handle new users and new items. We return to that in lesson 5.

blocks.title: A toy rating matrix: 5 users, 5 films, 6 blanks

scenes.caption: Ratings from 1 to 5. Grey cells were never rated: 6 of 25 cells are blank. Space1 and Space2 are sci-fi, Heist is a crime film, Rom1 and Rom2 are romances.
Look down the columns. Users who rate Space1 high also rate Space2 high, and the two romances move together. That co-movement is the signal CF exploits.
The question for this lesson: Eve never rated Space2. What should we predict for that blank cell, using only other people's ratings?

blocks.md: **Item-to-item CF** (Sarwar et al. 2001; Linden, Smith and York at Amazon, 2003) compares *columns*. Linden et al. treat each item as a vector whose dimensions are customers, and compare two items with the cosine of the angle between their vectors. The expensive part, a **similar-items table**, is built offline. Online, the system only looks up neighbours of the few items this user touched, so the cost depends on the user's history, not on the catalog size or number of customers.

blocks.tex: \operatorname{sim}(i,j)=\cos(\vec r_i,\vec r_j)=\frac{\vec r_i\cdot\vec r_j}{\lVert\vec r_i\rVert\,\lVert\vec r_j\rVert}
blocks.caption: Item-item cosine. Here a blank counts as 0, as in Linden et al.'s customer vectors.

blocks.title: Item-item similarity: plain cosine vs adjusted cosine

scenes.caption: Plain cosine on the columns of the rating matrix. Space1 and Space2 score 0.75, Rom1 and Rom2 score 0.95: the genres show up as blocks.
But every pair is positive, even Space1 and Rom1 at 0.28. Ratings are all positive numbers, so even opposite tastes share direction.
Adjusted cosine (Sarwar et al.) first subtracts each user's mean rating and uses only users who rated both items. Now Space1 and Rom1 score -0.97: opposite tastes.

blocks.md: To predict, Sarwar et al. take the user's ratings on the *k* items most similar to the target and form a similarity-weighted average:

blocks.caption: N_k(i;u): the k items most similar to i among those u has rated.

blocks.prompt: Eve rated Space1 = 5, Heist = 4 and Rom1 = 1. With plain cosine, Space2's similarities to those are 0.75, 0.45 and 0.19. Using the k = 2 most similar items, what do we predict for Eve on Space2?
blocks.reveal: The two neighbours are Space1 and Heist: $(0.75 \times 5 + 0.45 \times 4) / (0.75 + 0.45) \approx 4.63$ (unrounded similarities). Eve likes sci-fi and crime, so a high score is sensible. Rom1 was dropped because it is the least similar of the rated items.

blocks.md: Treating a blank as a rating of 0 is a modelling choice, not a fact. It makes plain cosine reward items that are merely *rated by the same people*, whatever the ratings. In Sarwar et al.'s MovieLens experiments, adjusted cosine gave lower error (MAE) than plain cosine or Pearson correlation.
Item-to-item CF scales because the heavy work (the similar-items table) is offline, and the online step only touches the handful of items in one user's history.

blocks.question: Amazon's item-to-item design is described as fast even for huge catalogs. What makes the online request cheap?
options: Its cost depends on how many items this user has bought or rated, because neighbours are looked up in a precomputed table
It compares the user with every other customer, but uses cosine, which is cheap
It clusters customers into segments and only scores the user's segment
It recomputes item similarities for each request using only popular items
blocks.explain: Linden et al. build the similar-items table offline (worst case O(N^2 M), closer to O(NM) in practice). The online step aggregates neighbours of the user's own items, so it scales independently of catalog size and customer count.

blocks.question: With plain cosine and blanks as 0, Space1 and Rom1 come out at +0.28 although fans of one rate the other 1 star. Why?
options: Cosine is undefined for rating data, so the value is noise
All ratings are positive, so any two items rated by the same users share direction; adjusted cosine removes each user's mean first
The users who rated both items gave them identical ratings
Rom1 has more ratings than Space1, which inflates the cosine
blocks.explain: With non-negative entries the cosine can never be negative. Subtracting each user's average rating (adjusted cosine) turns 'rated 1 by a sci-fi fan' into a negative number, and the similarity becomes -0.97.

lessons.title: Matrix factorization: learning user and item vectors

blocks.md:
Neighbourhood methods compare raw rows or columns. **Latent factor models** instead learn a short vector for every user and every item, so that their dot product predicts the rating. In Koren, Bell and Volinsky's words, both are mapped to a joint latent factor space of dimension *f*. For films the factors may line up with things like comedy vs drama, or be uninterpretable.

Recall from the embeddings course that an embedding is a trainable lookup table. Here there are two tables: users P and items Q.

blocks.caption: Koren et al., equations 1 and 2. The sum runs only over known ratings (the set kappa); lambda penalizes large vectors to avoid overfitting.

blocks.md:
Only observed cells enter the loss. Earlier systems filled the blanks first (imputation), which Koren et al. note is expensive and can distort the data. Two algorithms minimize this loss.

**Stochastic gradient descent** (popularized by Simon Funk) loops over known ratings, computes the error $e_{ui}=r_{ui}-q_i^{\top}p_u$, and nudges just those two vectors:

blocks.tex: q_i\leftarrow q_i+\gamma\,(e_{ui}\,p_u-\lambda q_i),\qquad p_u\leftarrow p_u+\gamma\,(e_{ui}\,q_i-\lambda p_u)
blocks.caption: Koren et al.'s SGD update with learning rate gamma. In our toy: f = 2, gamma = 0.05, lambda = 0.1, vectors initialized to 1 plus Gaussian noise (sd 0.3, seed 0).

blocks.title: One SGD step on Ana's rating of Space1

scenes.caption: Take the training pair (Ana, Space1, 5). Before training, the vectors are close to [1, 1].
The model predicts 1.816, so the error is 3.184: far too low.
The item vector moves toward the user vector, scaled by the error. The old copy is kept so both updates use the same starting point.
The user vector moves toward the item vector. The new prediction is 2.428: one step closed part of the gap, and only these two vectors changed.

blocks.title: Predicted ratings P Q^T as SGD runs (19 known ratings)

scenes.caption: Epoch 0: every prediction is near 1 to 3 because the vectors start near [1, 1]. Training RMSE 2.15.
Epoch 1 (19 updates): everything drifts up toward the average rating. RMSE 1.83.
Epoch 5: still mostly a global offset; the model has not split users by taste yet. RMSE 1.63.
Epoch 20: users start to differ (Ben's Space2 is 4.7, Dee's 1.5), but the split is still messy: romance fan Dee gets 4.6 for Space1. RMSE 1.31.
Epoch 50: the two taste groups are clear. RMSE 0.39.
Epoch 100: RMSE 0.35. The boxed cells were never rated; these are the recommendations. Eve on Space2 gets 5.0, close to item-item's 4.63.

blocks.md: Read the learned item vectors: Space1 = [0.23, 2.26], Rom1 = [2.08, 0.02]. One coordinate became a romance axis and the other a sci-fi and action axis, although nobody told the model about genres. That is what collaborative filtering learns from behaviour alone.

**Alternating least squares** (ALS) uses a different observation. The loss is not convex in P and Q together, but if Q is fixed it is an ordinary ridge regression in each $p_u$, with a closed-form solution, and vice versa. ALS alternates: solve all users, then all items. Each step cannot increase the loss.

blocks.caption: Q_u: the rows of Q for items u rated; r_u: u's ratings. The item step is the same with roles swapped. This solve penalizes each vector once; eq. 2's per-rating penalty would use n_u lambda I.

blocks.title: Training RMSE: SGD epochs vs ALS sweeps (same start)

scenes.caption: SGD needs many passes over the 19 ratings on this toy; it lingers near the global offset for about 20 epochs before the factors split.
ALS solves each vector exactly given the others: RMSE 0.70 after one sweep, 0.33 after ten. Each sweep costs more than one SGD epoch (small matrix solves), so this is not a wall-clock comparison.

blocks.md: Koren et al. call SGD generally easier and faster, and name two cases where ALS wins: when you can **parallelize** (every $p_u$ is solved independently of the other users) and when the data is **implicit**, where the training set is dense and looping over every cell is impractical. That second case is the next lesson.

**Biases.** Much of a rating is not interaction at all: some users rate harshly and some films are better. Koren et al. add a global mean and per-user and per-item offsets, $\hat r_{ui}=\mu+b_i+b_u+q_i^{\top}p_u$. Their example: mean 3.7, Titanic rated 0.5 above average, Joe 0.3 below other users, so the baseline estimate is 3.9 before any factors.

Look at Dee on Space1 at epoch 100: -0.2, below the 1 to 5 scale. A bare dot product is unconstrained and our tiny model has no bias terms, so extrapolated cells can land off the scale. Production systems add biases and clip predictions; for ranking only the order matters.

blocks.question: After one SGD update on the training pair (Ana, Space1), which parameters changed?
options: All user vectors, because the loss sums over everyone
Only Q[Space1]
Only P[Ana] and Q[Space1]
Every item vector Ana has rated
blocks.explain: The squared error for one rating depends only on p_u and q_i (plus their regularizers), so the stochastic gradient is zero for every other parameter. That is why SGD steps are cheap.

blocks.question: You have billions of implicit events (every user-item pair counts) and a cluster of machines. Which optimizer do Koren et al. suggest, and why?
options: SGD, because it is always faster than ALS
Neither; matrix factorization cannot use implicit data
SGD with a larger learning rate, to make up for the dense data
ALS, because each user (and each item) vector is an independent least-squares solve that parallelizes, and it avoids looping over every cell of a dense matrix
blocks.explain: Both reasons are stated in the paper: ALS parallelizes naturally, and for implicit data the training set is not sparse, so per-cell SGD loops are impractical. Hu et al. show how ALS stays linear in the number of non-zeros.

lessons.title: Implicit feedback: preference, confidence and weighted ALS

blocks.md: Most real signals are implicit: watches, clicks, purchases. Hu, Koren and Volinsky (ICDM 2008) list what makes them different. There is no negative feedback: a show you never watched may be one you dislike, or one you never heard of. The data is noisy: you may watch because the channel stayed on. And the numbers measure **confidence**, not preference: a show watched every week tells you more than one watched once.

Their model splits each observation $r_{ui}$ (for example minutes or times watched) into two parts:

- a binary **preference** $p_{ui}=1$ if $r_{ui}>0$, else 0;
- a **confidence** $c_{ui}=1+\alpha r_{ui}$, so unwatched cells still count, but only weakly.

In their TV experiments, $\alpha=40$ worked well. They also describe a log scaling $c_{ui}=1+\alpha\log(1+r_{ui}/\epsilon)$ for heavy-tailed counts.

blocks.caption: The sum runs over ALL user-item pairs, not just observed ones. x_u: user factors, y_i: item factors.

blocks.title: From watch counts to preference and confidence (alpha = 40)

scenes.caption: Raw implicit data: how many times each user watched each title. Zeros are not dislikes; they are unknowns.
Preference p: 1 wherever the count is positive. A single accidental watch (Ana on Rom2) looks exactly like eight deliberate ones (Ana on Space1).
Confidence c = 1 + 40 r. Ana-Space1 now weighs 321 and Ana-Rom2 weighs 41, and every unwatched cell keeps weight 1: a weak vote for 'probably not'.

blocks.md: Because every cell is in the loss, there are m x n terms (users times items) and SGD over cells is out. Hu et al. use ALS. With Y fixed, each user's vector has a closed form, and a simple identity removes the dense part of the cost:

blocks.caption: C^u is diagonal with c_ui. Y^T Y is the same for every user, computed once; C^u - I is non-zero only on the n_u items u touched.

blocks.md: So one user costs $O(f^2 n_u+f^3)$ and a full sweep costs $O(f^2N+f^3m)$, where N is the number of non-zero observations: linear in the input, even though the loss covers every cell. Hu et al. report typical f between 20 and 200 and about 10 sweeps. Google's recommendation course teaches a closely related method under the name **WALS** (weighted alternating least squares).

blocks.prompt: New user Fay watched Space1 10 times and each romance once (probably autoplay). Keep the item vectors from lesson 2 fixed and solve for Fay's vector. With alpha = 0 (every cell weight 1), which title gets Fay's LOWEST score?
blocks.reveal: Space1, the film watched ten times, at 0.26. With equal weights, two romance watches outvote one sci-fi watch, so the solve lands on a romance-leaning vector [0.42, 0.07]. Confidence weighting fixes this, as the next figure shows.

blocks.title: Fay's scores x_u^T y_i for each title, as alpha grows

scenes.caption: alpha = 0: preference only. Rom1 and Rom2 score 0.88 and 0.85, Space1 only 0.26. The model has read Fay as a romance fan.
alpha = 1: Space1's confidence is 11 vs 2 for each romance. Space1 rises to 0.86 and the unwatched Space2 tops the list at 1.06.
alpha = 40 (Hu et al.'s value): Space1 = 1.00, close to its target of 1, and Space2 is recommended first at 1.22. Note the scores are preferences, not star ratings.

blocks.md: Do not drop the zeros. Training only on observed implicit events (all with p = 1) lets the model predict 1 everywhere and still reach zero loss. The low-confidence zeros are what make the scores discriminative.
Implicit feedback = preference (did it happen) x confidence (how sure we are). The confidence weights decide which events the factors must explain.

blocks.question: In Hu et al.'s model, what does a cell with r_ui = 0 contribute to the loss?
options: Nothing: unobserved cells are skipped, as in explicit matrix factorization
A strong push toward a negative rating of -1
A term with target p = 0 and minimum confidence c = 1, a weak signal that u probably does not prefer i
A term whose weight is set by the item's popularity
blocks.explain: With c = 1 + alpha r, a zero count gives c = 1: the cell is in the loss with target 0 but much less weight than observed events, reflecting that a missing event has many possible causes.

blocks.question: Why does the identity Y^T C^u Y = Y^T Y + Y^T (C^u - I) Y matter?
options: It makes the loss convex in X and Y jointly
It lets each user update cost depend on that user's n_u touched items instead of all n items, so a sweep is linear in the number of non-zeros
It removes the need for regularization
It turns ALS into SGD
blocks.explain: Y^T Y is shared and precomputed once per sweep. The user-specific correction only involves rows with c_ui different from 1, which are the items the user touched.

lessons.title: Two-stage systems: candidate generation, two towers, ranking

blocks.md: Scoring every item for every request does not scale to millions of items. Covington, Adams and Sargin's YouTube paper (RecSys 2016) describes the standard split: **candidate generation** narrows millions of videos to hundreds using broad collaborative signals, then **ranking** scores those hundreds with a richer model and many more features, and a few dozen are shown. Other candidate sources can be blended in before ranking.

blocks.title: The two-stage recommender (after Covington et al., Figure 2)

scenes.caption: A request arrives with the user's history and context. The corpus is too large to score with an expensive model.
Candidate generation embeds the user and finds the nearest item vectors by dot product (approximate nearest neighbour). Cheap per item, so it can cover millions.
A few hundred candidates, plus some from other sources, go to the ranker, which can afford hundreds of features per item.
The ranker orders them and a few dozen are shown. Simplified: production stacks add filtering, business rules and diversity steps.

blocks.md: YouTube's candidate generator treats recommendation as **extreme multiclass classification**: predict which of millions of videos the user watches next, with a softmax over item embeddings $v_j$ given a user embedding $u$ built by a deep network from averaged watch and search embeddings plus features. Training uses **sampled softmax**: several thousand sampled negatives per example, corrected by importance weighting, which the paper says is more than 100 times faster than a full softmax. At serving time the softmax is dropped and candidates come from nearest neighbour search in the dot-product space.

**Two-tower models** (Yi et al., RecSys 2019, also YouTube) put features on both sides: a query tower maps user and context features to $u(x)$, an item tower maps item features (ID, content) to $v(y)$. Both outputs are L2-normalized and scored as $s(x,y)=\langle u,v\rangle/\tau$, with temperature $\tau$ tuned. Item embeddings are precomputed and indexed, so serving is still one nearest neighbour lookup.

Training with **in-batch negatives** is cheap: in a batch of B (user, item) pairs, each user's positive is scored against the other B - 1 items in the batch.

blocks.tex: P_B(y_i\mid x_i)=\frac{e^{s^c(x_i,y_i)}}{\sum_{j\in B} e^{s^c(x_i,y_j)}},\qquad s^c(x_i,y_j)=s(x_i,y_j)-\log p_j
blocks.caption: Yi et al.'s batch softmax with the logQ correction. p_j: the probability that item j appears in a random batch.

blocks.md:
Why correct? Batches are drawn from real traffic, so popular items appear as *negatives* far more often than a uniform sample would put them there. Yi et al.: popular items are overly penalized as negatives. Subtracting $\log p_j$ (a larger boost for rare items) undoes that sampling bias.

Our toy: 3 genre features (sci-fi, romance, crime) per item; each user's input is their mean-centred ratings times genres; each tower is a fixed 3x3 matrix chosen by hand to stand in for a trained network; $\tau = 0.2$.

blocks.title: In-batch logits s = <u, v> / 0.2 for a batch of 4 pairs

scenes.caption: Rows are users, columns are the batch's positive items: Ana watched Space2, Ben Space1, Cal Rom1, Eve Heist. The diagonal holds the positives; every off-diagonal cell is used as a negative.
Ana and Ben are both sci-fi fans, so Ben's positive Space1 is a near-duplicate negative for Ana (logit 3.05 vs the positive 2.90). In-batch negatives can be items the user would like.
Assume streaming estimates p = 0.05, 0.30, 0.10, 0.02 for Space2, Space1, Rom1, Heist (Space1 is the hit). Subtract log p from each column: rare Heist gains 3.91, popular Space1 only 1.20.

blocks.title: Ana's in-batch softmax: plain vs logQ-corrected

scenes.caption: Plain batch softmax: the popular Space1 takes 0.484 of the mass, more than Ana's positive (0.419). The gradient pushes Space1 down for Ana, and a hit lands in far more batches, so it is pushed down far more often than a rare item.
Corrected: Space1 falls to 0.109 and the positive rises to 0.565. Loss on Ana's row drops from 0.87 to 0.57; Ben's row (whose positive is Space1) rises from 0.77 to 2.26.

blocks.md: Yi et al. estimate $p_j$ on a stream without a fixed vocabulary. Two hashed arrays: A[h(y)] holds the last step at which y was seen, B[h(y)] a running estimate of the gap between sightings. When y appears at step t, $B\leftarrow(1-\alpha)B+\alpha(t-A)$, then $A\leftarrow t$, and $\hat p=1/B$. Their example: an item sampled every 50 steps has p = 0.02.

blocks.title: Streaming frequency estimate for one item (alpha = 0.5)

scenes.caption: Before the item appears, both slots hold 0. In real use alpha is small; 0.5 here so the estimate settles in a few steps.
Seen at step 48. The gap sample is 48 - 0, so B = 0.5 x 0 + 0.5 x 48 = 24: an overestimate of frequency (1/24) because B started at 0.
Seen at step 149: gap 46, B = 42.75.
Seen at step 201: gap 52, B = 47.38.
Seen at step 252: gap 51, B = 49.19, so p is about 0.0203: close to the true rate of one sighting per 50 steps (0.02).

blocks.md: **Ranking** sees only hundreds of candidates, so it can use hundreds of features. Covington et al. rank by predicted **expected watch time**, not click probability, which would favour clickbait. They train a weighted logistic regression: clicked impressions are weighted by watch time, unclicked ones by 1. The learned odds are then approximately $E[T](1+P)$, close to $E[T]$ when the click probability P is small, and serving uses $e^{Wx+b}$ as the score.
Retrieval must be cheap per item (dot products over precomputed vectors); ranking can be expensive per item. In-batch negatives are sampled by popularity, so correct each logit by log p_j.

blocks.question: A two-tower model trained with plain in-batch softmax rarely retrieves the top-100 hit items, even for users who like them. What is the most likely cause?
options: Hit items appear in many batches, so they are used as negatives far more often and get pushed down; apply the logQ correction
The temperature is too high, so all scores are equal
Hit items have too few training examples
Normalizing embeddings removes popularity information
blocks.explain: In-batch negatives follow the traffic distribution, which is power-law. Yi et al. note popular items are overly penalized as negatives and subtract log p_j from each logit to correct the bias.

blocks.question: Why does YouTube's ranker weight clicked impressions by watch time instead of predicting click probability?
options: Watch time is easier to log than clicks
Logistic regression cannot learn click probabilities
Click probability rewards deceptive videos that users do not finish; weighting by watch time makes the learned odds approximate expected watch time
Weighting makes the model train faster
blocks.explain: Covington et al. say ranking by click-through rate promotes deceptive videos users do not complete (clickbait), while watch time better captures engagement. The weighting makes the odds approximately E[T](1 + P).

lessons.title: Cold start: content for new items, bandits for new users

blocks.md: A pure ID-based model has no row for a user it never saw and no column for an item uploaded a minute ago. Google's recommendation course puts it bluntly: an item not seen in training has no embedding, so the model cannot score it. Yet fresh content matters: Covington et al. say users prefer fresh content and add an "example age" feature so the model can learn how popularity changes over time.

**New item, three fixes in increasing order of data.**

1. *Content heuristic*: average the embeddings of items from the same category or uploader (from Google's course).
2. *Content tower*: if the item tower reads content features, a new item gets a vector from its features alone. Yi et al. motivate two towers partly by this: content features help with sparse data and skewed popularity.
3. *Projection*: once a few users interact, solve one ALS step for the new item with the user vectors fixed, without retraining the model.

blocks.caption: One ALS (WALS) step for a new item: S is the set of users who rated it, P_S their fixed vectors from lesson 2.

blocks.title: Predicted ratings for a brand-new sci-fi film, Space3

scenes.caption: Day zero, ID-only model: Space3 has no item vector, so it cannot be scored or retrieved at all.
Category average: q = mean of Space1 and Space2 vectors = [0.52, 2.19]. Sci-fi fans Ana, Ben, Eve get 4.4, 4.3, 5.0; Cal and Dee are low. Values clipped to 1 to 5.
After Ana rates it 5 and Cal rates it 1, one ALS step gives q = [0.18, 2.50]: Ben now 4.7, Eve at the cap. Two ratings sharpened the contrast. Clipped to 1 to 5.

blocks.md: The two-tower version needs no ratings at all: Space3's content (sci-fi, a little crime) goes through the item tower from lesson 4, and the cosine with each user's vector is Ana 0.60, Ben 0.84, Cal -0.65, Dee -0.70, Eve 0.78. The same users come out on top, now from features alone.

**New user.** With no history, there is nothing to put into the user tower but context (device, country, time). Covington et al. note that demographic features provide priors so recommendations behave reasonably for new users. A safe first answer is **popularity**: Hu et al. found that simply ranking by popularity was a surprisingly strong baseline on their TV data. But popularity never learns what *this* kind of user likes, and items that are never shown never collect data.

That is an exploration problem. Li, Chu, Langford and Schapire (WWW 2010) treat news recommendation for new users and changing content as a **contextual bandit**, and propose **LinUCB**.

blocks.caption: LinUCB with disjoint models: A_a starts as the identity and adds x x^T when arm a is shown; b_a adds reward times x. Show the arm with the highest p.

blocks.title: The exploration bonus shrinks as an arm is shown more

scenes.caption: With a single constant feature, A = 1 + n, so the bonus is alpha / sqrt(1 + n). An arm never shown keeps the full bonus alpha, so it gets tried.
Larger alpha explores longer before trusting the estimate; smaller alpha exploits sooner. Li et al. treat alpha as a parameter to tune.

blocks.md: A toy run (seed 0): 4 arms, context x = [1, is_mobile], users split 50/50 mobile and desktop, alpha = 1, ties broken by popularity. True click rates (unknown to the algorithm): mobile users like Rom1 best (0.40), desktop users Space1 (0.30). The popular Space1 is wrong for mobile users.

blocks.title: How often LinUCB showed each arm

scenes.caption: Step 1: every arm has estimate 0 and the same bonus (1 for desktop, 1.41 for mobile), a four-way tie. The popularity prior breaks it: show Space1. That is popularity as the cold-start default.
After 10 users: counts [3, 1, 5, 1]. Every arm has been tried, because unshown arms keep a large bonus.
After 200: counts [82, 9, 55, 54]. For a mobile user Rom1 now has estimate 0.37 and a small bonus 0.14, so it wins mobile traffic.
After 2000: Rom1 mostly to mobile, Space1 mostly to desktop. 670 clicks (0.335 per user) vs expected 0.225 for always-popular and 0.35 for the best possible policy.

blocks.md: Space2 was shown only 23 times in 2000, although it is mobile users' second choice (0.25). Optimism-based exploration stops exploring once an arm looks clearly worse than the leader; that is the point, but it means some items get little data. Freshness boosts or explicit exploration slots are common additions.
Cold start is a data problem, so the fixes are other data: content features for new items, context and popularity for new users, then controlled exploration to collect the interactions CF needs.

blocks.question: A new item has rich metadata but zero interactions. Which model can rank it on day one?
options: Matrix factorization with an ID embedding table, retrained nightly
Item-to-item CF using co-purchase cosine
A two-tower model whose item tower reads content features
LinUCB with the item's ID as the only feature
blocks.explain: ID-based MF and co-purchase similarity both need interactions involving the item. An item tower over content features produces a vector from metadata alone, which can be indexed and retrieved immediately.

blocks.question: In LinUCB, an arm has never been shown. What is its score p for any context x?
options: 0, so it is never chosen until an exploration phase
alpha times the norm of x, since A is the identity and b is zero, so it is likely to be tried
Its popularity
Undefined until the arm gets one reward
blocks.explain: With A_a = I and b_a = 0, theta is 0 and the bonus is alpha sqrt(x^T x). Unseen arms therefore carry the largest uncertainty bonus, which is how LinUCB explores new items.

blocks.question: Why not serve only the most popular items to every new user forever?
options: Popularity is a weak baseline that rarely beats random
Popularity cannot be computed in real time
It violates the cold-start assumption that new users have no context
It never collects feedback on other items or learns what each kind of user prefers; in our toy it earns 0.225 clicks per user vs 0.335 for LinUCB
blocks.explain: Popularity is a strong default (Hu et al. call it surprisingly powerful), but it is the same for everyone and is a feedback loop: unshown items stay unshown. A bandit trades a little short-term reward for information.

blocks.md: Offline evaluation hides the rating or event you want to predict, recommends, and scores the list with a ranking metric such as recall@k or NDCG (from the ranking metrics course). The traps are in *what* you hide and *what* you compare against.

scenes.caption: Each block is one interaction, in time order. Space3 and Rom3 are released in week 8.
Random holdout: test events (cyan) are scattered. To predict Ana's week-3 Space2 the model trains on Ana's weeks 6 and 8, and on Space3's later popularity: future information.
Temporal split: train on everything before week 8, test on weeks 8 and 9. This is the situation the deployed model faces, including items it has never seen.

blocks.md: Covington et al. call this out directly: many CF systems hold out a random item and predict it from the rest of the history, which leaks future information and ignores asymmetric consumption (episodes are watched in order; people find an artist's popular work before the niche). Predicting the **next** watch from only earlier actions performed much better in their A/B tests. Hu et al. trained on four weeks of TV viewing and tested on the following week, and removed shows a user had already watched in training, because those were "easy" predictions.

A synthetic check (seed 0): 500 users, 40 items, 10 time steps, 5015 events; item popularity is skewed and drifts over time, and the top 5 items take 68% of all events. We evaluate recall@5 of popularity recommenders, excluding items the user already had in training.

scenes.caption: Temporal split (train steps 0 to 7, test 8 and 9). Random recommendations: 0.14. All-time popularity: 0.70, five times better. Popularity bias makes this baseline hard to beat.
Counting only the last two training steps scores 0.86: when tastes drift, freshness matters. This is why YouTube feeds example age as a feature.
The same all-time model under a random 20% holdout scores 0.52, not 0.70. The split changed the task, so this number does not predict deployment, and 'recent' is not even well defined on it.

blocks.md: A gap between a random-split number and a temporal-split number is not a bug in either; they measure different tasks. Only the temporal one resembles what the system will face, so compare models on that.

**Weak baselines.** Dacrema, Cremonesi and Jannach (RecSys 2019) tried to reproduce 18 neural top-n recommendation algorithms from top venues. Only 7 could be reproduced with reasonable effort, and 6 of those could often be beaten by simple, well-tuned nearest-neighbour or graph-based methods. Always include tuned popularity, item-item CF and matrix factorization baselines.

**Feedback loops.** Logged data comes from what the old system chose to show, so popular items collect even more evidence; Covington et al. note that machine learning systems are biased toward the past and that new content must be able to surface. Offline metrics guide iteration, but Covington et al. rely on live A/B tests for the final call, since offline precision does not always track engagement such as watch time.
Split by time, exclude what the user already consumed, beat tuned simple baselines, and confirm with an online experiment.

blocks.question: Your new model beats matrix factorization on a random 80/20 holdout of watch events. Before shipping, what is the most important check?
options: Re-run with a different random seed for the same 80/20 split
Evaluate with a temporal split (train on the past, predict later events) against tuned baselines, then A/B test
Switch the metric from recall@k to RMSE
Add more epochs until offline recall stops improving
blocks.explain: A random holdout lets the model see a user's future and future popularity. A temporal split matches deployment, tuned simple baselines guard against weak comparisons (Dacrema et al.), and only an online test measures the real effect.

blocks.question: In Hu et al.'s TV evaluation, why were shows the user had already watched in training removed from the test set?
options: People rewatch the same shows weekly, so predicting them is easy and would inflate the score without testing discovery
They were too rare to matter
They made the percentile ranking undefined
The confidence weights for them were zero
blocks.explain: Hu et al. note the tendency to repeatedly watch the same programs and remove these 'easy' predictions so the evaluation measures recommending something new.
